search_result.text:
Tokyo —

Former Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe is in critical condition and fighting for his life after being shot in the street in broad daylight while making a campaign speech in the central city of Nara, in an attack that has shocked the nation.

Prime Minister Fumio Kishida said in a press conference on Friday that Abe is receiving emergency treatment at the Nara Medical University hospital, where medical staff are fighting to save him.

“This is not a forgivable act,” Kishida said. “We will comprehend the situation and take appropriate measures.”

Abe’s younger brother, Japan’s Defense Minister Nobuo Kishi told reporters Abe was receiving a blood transfusion. Shortly afterward, Abe’s wife arrived at the hospital to be with her husband, Japan’s public broadcaster NHK reported.

An official from the Nara City Fire Department earlier confirmed to CNN that Abe was in a state of cardiopulmonary arrest, a term used to describe the sudden loss of heart function and breathing.

An aerial photo shows a man believed to be former Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe on the stretcher at Nara Medical University Hospital in Kashihara, Nara Prefecture on July 8. Shohei Izumi/The Yomiuri Shimbun/AP

Abe is the former Liberal Democratic Party leader and Japan’s longest-serving prime minister, holding office from 2006 to 2007 and again from 2012 to 2020, before resigning due to health reasons. Since stepping down, he has remained in the public eye and regularly appears in the media to discuss current affairs.

Abe was rushed to hospital via helicopter in the aftermath of the shooting. According to police, he was believed to have been shot twice, in the chest and neck, NHK reported.

A suspect, identified as Tetsuya Yamagami, a local man in his 40s, was arrested and charged with attempted murder, according to NHK. It appears the suspect used a handmade gun in the attack, though the motive remains unclear. He is being held for questioning at Nara Nishi police station, NHK reported.

Photos from the scene show the weapon on the ground, wrapped in black material.

CNN has not yet been able to independently verify these reports.

Video aired on NHK and images from the scene show police wrestling a man to the ground near where the former Prime Minister was standing. Another video aired by NHK shows smoke in the air.

What appears to be a homemade weapon on the ground near where a security officer seized a suspect believed to have shot former Prime Minister Shinzo Abe in front of Yamatosaidaiji Station on July 8, in Nara, Japan. Asahi Shimbun/Getty Images

Prime Minister Kishida, who was on a tour of duty, rushed back to his office and government ministers in various parts of the country had been urged to return to Tokyo immediately, Chief Cabinet Secretary Hirokazu Matsuno said.

“Such barbaric behavior is unacceptable for any reason and we firmly condemn it. The government will take all possible measures to deal with the situation,” Matsuno said.

How events unfolded

Abe was making a speech in support of LDP candidates ahead of the upcoming Upper House elections scheduled for Sunday. He was due to head to Kyoto and Saitama prefecture, near the capital Tokyo.

Video aired by NHK captured the moments leading up to the shooting and show Abe speaking to a small crowd in the street in front of Yamatosaidaiji Station in Nara. In subsequent video two shots can be heard.

In this aerial image, former Prime Minister Shinzo Abe is on a stretcher to a helicopter after being shot in front of Yamatosaidaiji Station on July 8. The Asahi Shimbun/Getty Images

The former Prime Minister was conscious and responsive while being transported following the shooting, police sources told NHK.

Images show Abe being carried on a stretcher to a helicopter.

Outpouring of global concern

World leaders sent well wishes and messages of condolence in the wake of the shooting.

The United States Ambassador to Japan Rahm Emmanuel said in a tweet early Friday, “We are all saddened and shocked by the shooting of former Prime Minister Abe Shinzo.”

“Abe-san has been an outstanding leader of Japan and unwavering ally of the US The US Government and American people are praying for the well-being of Abe-san, his family, & people of Japan.”

British Prime Minister Boris Johnson said he is “utterly appalled and saddened to hear about the despicable attack on Shinzo Abe,” while Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said he was “deeply distressed by the attack on my dear friend.”

Among those sharing messages of support and concern were US Secretary of State Antony Blinken, Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, and Mexico’s Foreign Minister Marcelo Ebrard.

Japan’s low gun crime

Abe’s shooting has shocked Japan, which has one of the lowest rates of gun crime in the world due to its extremely strict gun control laws.

In 2018, Japan only reported nine deaths from firearms, compared with 39,740 that year in the United States, according to data compiled by the Sydney School of Public Health at the University of Sydney.

Under Japan’s firearms laws, the only guns permitted for sale are shotguns and air rifles – handguns are outlawed. But getting them is a long and complicated process.

Nancy Snow, Japan director of the International Security Industrial Council, told CNN that Friday’s shooting will change the country “forever.”

“It’s not only rare, but it’s really culturally unfathomable,” Snow said. “The Japanese people can’t imagine having a gun culture like we have in the United States. This is a speechless moment. I really feel at a loss for words. I pray for the best for the former prime minister.”

Updated July 19, 2026, 11:02 p.m. ET

Spain claimed its second World Cup title, defeating Lionel Messi and Argentina 1-0 after extra time at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey – crushing the defending champions’ dreams of a repeat.

La Roja always looked more likely to score but it took until the second period of extra time for Ferran Torres to blast home the winner on an assist from Nico Williams. That finally got the ball past goalkeeper Emi Martinez, who set a World Cup final record for saves.

Argentina didn’t manage a single shot on goal and didn’t even have its first attempt until late in the second period of stoppage time. Midfielder Enzo Fernandez was sent off in the 93rd minute for his second yellow card, putting Argentina down to 10 men for the entirety of extra time.

Argentina was trying to become just the third team in history to repeat as World Cup champion, and the first since Brazil defended its title in 1962 and this almost certainly marks the final appearance for the 39-year-old Messi, considered the greatest soccer player in world history.

The 2030 World Cup will be co-hosted by Spain, Portugal and Morocco – with Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay also each hosting an opening match to celebrate the 100th anniversary of the inaugural tournament.

Spain defender Pau Cubarsi won the World Cup's Best Young Player award after the 19-year-old helped his team keep seven clean sheets in the tournament.

search_result.title: World Cup final live — Spain wins its way, with defensive precision
search_result.text:
Updated July 19, 2026, 9:49 p.m. ET

North Jersey welcomes fans to the World Cup final on Sunday, July 19 at New York New Jersey Stadium, aka MetLife Stadium.

It's Argentina, led by Lionel Messi, who has had his ups and downs on the pitch in New Jersey, versus Spain, led by Mikel Oyarzabal, which searches for its first title since 2010. The kickoff is scheduled for 3 p.m. in East Rutherford, with sunny skies predicted over New Jersey, no rain anticipated.

Stadium gates open at 11 a.m.

We've got you covered on your trip to and from the stadium, and everything in between.

Whether you're watching the Spain versus Argentina match at MetLife Stadium, a watch party, a bar, or a neighborhood party on Sunday, check back here throughout the day.

We will bring you live coverage of this historic event in New Jersey.

Spain shows that defense is still king

Spain beat Argentina 1-0 in extra time at MetLife Stadium to claim its first World Cup title since 2010, and it did so by turning the world’s biggest tournament into a showcase of defensive precision. La Roja finished with 12 shots on goal in the final and didn’t allow Argentina a single one. The same Argentina that scored multiple goals in its seven other World Cup matches.

Spain finished with 65 percent possession and completed more than twice as many passes as Argentina. Its captain and midfield anchor summed up the team’s identity before the final.

“We're a very complete team,” said Rodri, who took home the Golden Ball as Player of the Tournament. “We're very difficult to defeat. We've shown this throughout the entire competition, conceding only one goal. We managed very well our box, the opponent's box and the middle of the park as well. So we don't have that many weaknesses.”

Here's the celebration of the winning goal

Want to take a second look at the celebration by Ferran Torres of Spain's winning goal? You can see it here in a series of photos, frame by frame:

What's being said about Lionel Messi

Coach Lionel Scaloni postgame: "He's 39 years old now. Unbelievable. There's nothing new to discover from my side. It was clear for me that he was going to play up until he decided not to do so. I hope that everyone feels proud of him and what he achieved. He's the best footballer ever to step on the pitch. What he did in the World Cup was incredible."

MetLife exit and President Trump 'freeze'

Steady stream of fans, mostly in Argentina jerseys, made their way out of the stadium and to the host committee buses at about 7 p.m. Dozens of buses were waiting to be filled with fans for transport to Nutley and three points in Manhattan.

As they filled, they left with little to no traffic at the stadium. That is expected to change as more buses and black car VIPs make their way out of MetLife.

The transportation “freeze” that takes place for President Trump and FLOTUS to leave the stadium went into effect at 6:54 p.m., meaning all roads and trains are frozen until cleared by US Secret Service. The freeze lasted seven minutes.

At 7 p.m., his motorcade was seen going over the Ramp D bridge and there was massive traffic at exit 16W, which was held for 10-15 minutes.

Trump’s entry to the stadium Sunday lasted 30 minutes.

That section of Spanish fans in the 200 level aren't going anywhere.

Spain is celebrated

The stadium announcer is calling each Spain player in turn to receive a champion's medal from Gianni Infantino and to kiss the trophy.

Lamine Yamal got the biggest cheer from the Spain fans, with a close second to Cubarsi.

Team captain Rodrigo Hernandez is the last to be recognized. He receives the trophy and gets thanked by President Donald Trump, who then goes to the side of the stage with Gianni Infantino.

Gold confetti is shooting out as the players jump around. Rodri is holding the trophy with one hand, and presents it to one of his teammates, and so on, and so on. Each one lowers the trophy, then raises it up and kisses it.

Meanwhile, Messi is slowly walking through the tunnel.

Awards handed out on MetLife pitch

First up in the postmatch celebration, the officials receive medals and pose for photos.

Spain defender Pau Cubarsi receives the FIFA Young Player Award. Je was born Jan. 22, 2007.

Spain midfielder and captain Rodri receives the Golden Ball as Player of the Tournament.

"Our goal when we got to this World Cup was to win the trophy," he said on Friday at Fanatics Fest in Manhattan. "We were convinced we could achieve it. We've shown this national team has been able to defeat great opponents."

Rodrigo "Rodri" Hernandez has won the Champions League with Manchester City and the Ballon D'Or as the top player in the world.

"The biggest thing you can achieve is becoming a world champion," he said on Friday at Fanatics Fest in Manhattan. "It's all part of the process. You have to get in the right mindset to achieve big things. That's the challenge we have rising to the top. I'm happy with my career, but there's always this extra ambition that makes you want to keep winning."

Golden Boot to Mbappe

France's Kylian Mbappe earns Golden Boot as 2026 World Cup top scorer.

Mbappe scored 10 goals during this year's World Cup, tying Gerd Muller, who also had 10 at the 1970 World Cup. Mbappe had a brace as France tried to come from behind against England in the third-place match but fell short in the high-scoring 6-4 affair on July 18 in Miami.

Celebration for Spain, heartbreak for Argentina

The Spain players are in two lines to the left of the new stage, closest to their fans. Argentina is clustered behind them.

There's a long double line of volunteers in neon green jackets behind the gigantic World Cup trophy.

The oversized white FIFA letters have been moved in front of the stage at the midfield line.

Argentina's players are slowly walking away toward the corner closest to their fans.

Here comes the trophy!

They're setting up for the trophy presentation on the MetLife Stadium pitch at 6:08 p.m. EST. There's a round, navy blue stage with the 2026 FIFA World Cup logo in it, and now it looks like they're building a bigger circle around it.

Spain wins second World Cup!

Despite a late push from Argentina, Spain wins the 2026 World Cup on a 1-0 score.

Striker Ferran Torres' goal stood and gave Spain its second World Cup.

This is the second consecutive World Cup where the defending champions lost in the final.

Spain becomes the first team in World Cup history to record seven shutouts in a single tournament. And by allowing one goal across eight matches, Spain set a World Cup record for the fewest allowed by a champion. France (1998), Italy (2006) and Spain (2010) all conceded two apiece en route to the title.

Messi gives Argentina opportunities late

Lionel Messi had two corners inside the extra five minutes of the final overtime period. The second corner turned into a shot opportunity but it flew high over the crossbar.

Second Spain goal called back

An offside called on Spain nixed a second goal that found the back of the net. It would have been Ferran Torres again, assist would have gone to Lamine Yamal.

Spain! Striker Ferran Torres scores to make it 1-0 coming out of the extra time halftime, 39 seconds in.

Torres runs to the corner closest to the Spain section in level 200. He also kicked the corner flag out of place.

Ferran Torres is the first sub to score in a World Cup final since 2014, when Mario Gotze of Germany beat … Argentina, according to an ESPN report.

Extra time halftime

Argentina versus Spain score remains as it did during regulation halftime: 0-0

No goal

Nico Williams' potential go-ahead goal is wiped off the board because of a foul by Spain's Mikel Merino leading up to the play.

Argentina and Spain reset for the extra time as Argentina plays a man down.

Argentina goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez made an 11th save shortly after the period began.

Those 11 saves sets a record for a World Cup final.

The last stop came just under three minutes into OT when Spain's Nico Williams poked a header toward the left post.

Late free kick stopped by Martinez

For his 10th save of the game, Argentina goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez made a crucial save to keep the game scoreless and shortly after, overtime.

The save came on a free kick from Spain's Lamine Yamal, who's now taken three shots and two on goal.

Martinez has been playing with a broken finger.

"Overcoming adversity is something we've been doing for the past three years," he said on Friday at Fanatics Fest in New York City. "Sometimes, I even feel like crying. I'm so grateful to life, to my family, these moments of joy. How can I explain this? We have to know how to enjoy this moment. Sometimes, as a professional footballer, we're not aware what's going on. My message to my teammates is to always remember this moment."

Red sends Enzo Fernandez off pitch

Enzo Fernandez gets his second yellow, and he's out. Argentina will play down a man for the rest of stoppage and any extra time.

Fernandez is walking off the field and into the tunnel. 90+3 minute.

The Argentine midfielder picked up his second yellow card in the third minute of stoppage time in the second half after a late tackle that left Spain's Pau Cubarsí spinning in the air.

Fernández was given his first yellow in the 82nd minute after yelling at an official over a no-call.

Emiliano Martinez has been busy

Argentina goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez has nine saves, the most since records began being kept in 1966. His ninth was a huge stop in extra time.

Tough defense by Spain

We're in the 79th minute and Argentina has zero shots on goal.

MetLife attendance for final on Sunday

It's a sellout, as expected. A crowd of 80,663. All but one of the Meadowlands matches have been sold out.

Spain and Argentina came back on the pitch at 4:20 p.m. EST.

Quick halftime show

Expected to be about a half hour in length, the halftime show lasted 11 minutes. The first half ended at 3:54 p.m. and the show went from 4:02 p.m. to 4:13 p.m.

What fans think at the half

Hector Jimenez Torres came from Mexico City hoping to find a ticket to the World Cup final. When prices remained out of reach, he settled in at Redd’s wearing an Argentina jersey with Lionel Messi’s name across the back.

Jimenez Torres, 56, had already attended World Cup matches in Philadelphia, Los Angeles and New Jersey. He arrived in the area Friday morning and also squeezed in a Yankees game, but the final was too expensive.

At halftime, with the match still scoreless, he said it may have been a little too technical for a neutral observer. He still gave Argentina a 50-50 chance.

Halftime show

There's a countdown on the scoreboard, less than three minutes to showtime. So it'll take less than a hydration break to get this party started.

Here's what Spain coach Luis de la Fuente said earlier this week when asked about the extended halftime:

"I think that everything that we consider to be strange or odd nowadays, you know, hydration breaks, this 30-minute halftime, maybe within 30 years will become normality. Maybe football is developing that way. We don't know. It is what it is. This is the situation we have. We need to adapt and we need to accept those things that you cannot change. We can't change that. So, we'll have to enjoy it."

Halftime

Spain and Argentina end the half in a scoreless tie.

Late first-half action

Argentina keeper Emiliano Martínez picks up his second save by stopping Spain leading scorer Mikel Oyarzabal in the 39th minute. Oyarzabal found free space at the top of the box and launched a low shot. The Argentines are still without a shot on goal after coming in with the tournament's highest-scoring offense

What's it like inside MetLife

The crowd seems a bit more subdued. It's also more mixed. Argentina is in the south end. The only clear Spain section in the 200 level behind the north end zone.

World Cup fever in North Jersey

We chatted with fans nearby New York New Jersey Stadium in East Rutherford. Here's what they had to say:

World Cup fans filed down Paterson Plank Road in Carlstadt on their way to the final at MetLife Stadium, walking past Redd’s Restaurant and Biergarten in Argentina jerseys, Spain colors and shirts bearing Lionel Messi’s name.

Among them was Robert Muñoz, 29, of Manhattan, who had waited until the walk to the stadium to buy his ticket.The price was $3,500, equivalent to nine months’ worth of savings.

Muñoz called the final a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity. The cost was easier to justify because the match was being played in his backyard, sparing him airfare and other travel expenses. Family members in Mexico had told him tickets there were also extremely expensive.

Still, he said FIFA needs to do something about ticket prices.

Dominic Thomas, 54, was also walking toward the stadium after traveling from Mumbai, India. He arrived in the New York area three days earlier and had attended Argentina’s semifinal victory over England in Miami.

Thomas and his friends bought their final tickets eight months ago. He was rooting for Spain, but said the team’s chances could depend on containing Messi.

“He is a genius,” Thomas said.

Delphina Hall, 26, of Santa Barbara, was attending with family members from Argentina. She said they take the national team seriously and wanted to be there for what could be Messi’s final game and was wearing his jersey as were the majority of fans making the hike.

Robert Verde, 29, a Venezuela native who lives in New York City, said he had been looking forward to the World Cup for three years and could not miss the final.

Verde was walking toward the stadium because he did not have a match ticket, which he said was required to board the train.

“I couldn’t miss this once-in-a-lifetime opportunity,” Verde said.

First save of the game goes to Argentina's Emiliano Martínez, who comes off his line in the fifth minute for a sliding stop on Lamine Yamal. Nice buildup from Spain to set up the chance.

That's dedication

Among the foreign fans in town for the Final was Anil Das, who drove eight-and-a-half hours overnight from Toronto to North Jersey. He left his home at 11:30 p.m. July 18 and arrived in the area at 8 a.m. the morning of the game, stopping only once.

“I didn’t sleep one second,” Das said. “I came, showered, and I’m all fired up. I want to see Argentina win.”

Das has been a fan of the team since the first game he watched on television with his father in 1986, when Argentina, led by Diego Maradona, won the World Cup.

Das held a banner with photos of both Maradona and Lionel Messi kissing the World Cup trophy, with the words “World Cup 2026 / Love You Dad.” The sign honored his late father, a former soccer player for India.

“It was his wish to see a game,” Das said. “Unfortunately he died early due to cancer.”

When asked his prediction for the game, Das, naturally was emphatic in wishing for a win for his favorite team.

“Argentina!” he exclaimed. “Maybe 2-1. Maybe more.”

Intros, national anthems and kickoff!

Added twist for the final: The flag was raised into the sky while the anthem was played.First Spain, then Argentina.

Stadium TV showed the teams lined up in the tunnel. Volunteers are pulling out the flags: Argentina in the south end zone and Spain in the north.

World Cup trophy shows off

The World Cup trophy is out on the pitch for all to see as the month-plus long tournament gets ready to finish its run, with Argentina versus Spain in East Rutherford, New Jersey at MetLife Stadium.

Mario Kempes, who won the Golden Boot with Argentina in 1978, has placed the trophy on a stand.

Actor Tom Cruise sets the stage for the finale.

National anthem

Jennifer Hudson sings the national anthem on the field with a special round FIFA logo for the final that has been laid out over the center circle, with a blue runway to the sideline.

People in what appear to be military uniforms are carrying the flags of the participating nations up the blue carpet and lining up around the circle.

There are people dressed in gold holding blue flags, and state police carrying the flags of New York, New Jersey, and the United States onto the blue carpet.

Pregame time!

We have warmups! Argentina is facing the south endzone of MetLife Stadium.

Here comes Spain wearing ... royal blue with orange stripes? Actually, they're donning large royal blue and black diamonds, cut with red-trimmed gold stripes.

Argentina superstar Lionel Messi waved to the MetLife crowd before starting warmups.

If you're wondering who was that singing "America the Beautiful" in a very operatic fashion, it was American tenor Christopher Macchio.

Here are the lineups for today's World Cup Final

We know one of the best players of all-time will be on the pitch in Argentina's Lionel Messi going head-to-head against Spain's young superstar in recently turned 19-year-old Lamine Yamal. Below is the rest of the lineup for Argentina and Spain:

Celebs in the house

A golf cart carrying New York Giants quarterback Jameis Winston made its way through the media entrance to the stadium at 1:20 p.m. Winston, who is working as a social correspondent for FOX Sports throughout the World Cup, sported a throwback U.S. men's national team jersey and was joyously singing from the back of the cart.

World Cup this and that

Priscila Damasceno was wearing a Brazil jersey. But her family had given her strict instructions to root for Argentina in the World Cup final.Not because they want the South American team to win. Quite the opposite.“All the countries I try, I give bad luck,” said Damasceno, who had rooted for her native Brazil, Mexico, and the United States during the tournament.

Will the offenses put on a show in World Cup Final?

If the 2026 World Cup has taught us anything, it’s that goals arrive in waves, late, and often. With 2.98 per game, this tournament is tracking to be the highest‑scoring edition since 1958 in Sweden (3.6). So the question hangs over MetLife Stadium: Will we get a high‑scoring final?

Argentina has poured in 19 goals, trailing only England and France (20 each). Only five teams have ever surpassed 20 in a World Cup. More striking: 13 of Argentina’s 19 goals have come after halftime, and 10 have arrived in the 80th minute or later.

Spain is the counterweight as a defensive juggernaut. La Roja enters the final on a 37‑match unbeaten run, tied for the longest in international history, and has conceded just one goal in seven World Cup matches, outscoring opponents 13-1. They became the first team ever to record six clean sheets in a single World Cup, and goalkeeper Unai Simón set the tournament record with 650 consecutive scoreless minutes.

Something has to give today in East Rutherford.

Paying up to get into MetLife

Luis Martinez, originally from Argentina, flew in from Orlando last night after buying a ticket for MetLife Stadium upward of $9,000 for the game.

Martinez said he was born into being a soccer fan — it’s “everything” to him. He also wants to see his favorite player, Messi, win a second title in what is likely his last World Cup.

“(Messi) did everything with his life and gave us everything,” Martinez said. “If Messi wins, everything will change because he demonstrates everything, what it means to be a good person, a good father, a good player. Everybody knows Messi. If you don't play soccer, you know Messi. We will see today the last dance of a very good human being.”

American Dream a meeting spot for World Cup fans

Fans are already filling up the confines of American Dream mall, both staking out spots for the watch party and killing time in the mall before heading over to the game.

A line of hundreds was forming outside the entrance to Fan Fest, where the ice rink typically is. Spanish and Argentinian flags are draped along the railings of the second and third levels of the mall. Lionel Messi jerseys are of course plentiful, but Lamine Yamal and Pedri can commonly be seen on the backs of Spanish supporters as well.

One group of Spanish citizens — Jose, Manuel, Inigo and Javier — met up from various places across Europe to attend the final. The four, decked out in different Spain jerseys, have traveled the globe to attend Spain’s World Cup matches across the last 16 years. They couldn’t get to South Africa in 2010, when Spain last won the World Cup, so a win over Argentina would be a lifetime highlight for the group.

“We cannot miss out this time. We had to be here to grab our tickets for the chance to win it and see what happens,” Manuel said.

Driving wasn't an option

Navin Gupta, of Long Island, drove to all the prior World Cup matches at New York-New Jersey Stadium, but figured today would be a “fiasco,” and opted for NJ Transit’s train. His son-in-law, had the worst commute of all trying to fly in from Florida amid the storms Monday night, getting in at 2 am.

World Cup this and that

Spain currently holds the Women’s World Cup title. If the men win today, it will be the first time the same nation has both trophies.

This is the first World Cup final between two Spanish-speaking nations since the first one in 1930, when host Uruguay beat Argentina.

Straight talking from World Cup fans

A quarter of fans from Merida, Mexico were very clear about who they supported in the World Cup final: Spain.

And it’s mainly about Argentina’s attitude.

“They treat us bad and speak bad about us,” said Rodrigo Cruz, pulling a new red jersey out of a brown paper bag and patting the crest.

“Even though their economy is a third of our economy.”

How travel to MetLife is going

With the festivities set to start well before kickoff, the host committee shuttles were up and running earlier than for previous matches as well. A line of five buses were ready and waiting for fans at the Nutley shuttle stop as of 10 a.m.

A few dozen fans moved seamlessly through the ticket scan and security checkpoint to board and make the short trip to nearby East Rutherford. Most fans were decked out in Argentina gear but some fans of Spain, and one in a Mexico jersey, were on hand as well.

Fans talked on the bus about the way the tournament has played out for Argentina, with one fan from Mexico saying he wasn’t rooting for Spain so much as rooting against Mexico. He joked that when fans went to the FIFA store and asked for Argentina jerseys, they were given referee shirts.

Head coaches no strangers

The relationship between Spanish coach Luis De La Fuente and Argentine coach Lionel Scaloni goes back decades. They met in 2017, after Scaloni retired as a player and enrolled to study for the UEFA Pro license, the highest coaching certification in European soccer.

The coach of Spain’s under-19 team at the time, De La Fuente was teaching the technique module. Scaloni still calls him “my mentor. De La Fuente has been Spain’s national team coach since 2022, after coming up through the youth system.

At Fanatics Fest on July 17, the two coaches embraced onstage. De La Fuente called the Argentinean “a close friend.” After at first declining to repeat what they’d told each other, Scaloni said, “I’m here because you are here.”Argentina’s head coach since 2018, Scaloni is the seventh coach to reach the World Cup final twice. Only Vittorio Pozzo of Italy won both times.

“He doesn’t know what I’m thinking when it comes to football. We haven’t really been talking about our playing style,” Scaloni said of De La Fuente. “Once they leave the hotel and are on the bus, I’m concerned as a coach. They’ve had this wonderful journey with Luis, so I am happy.”

Weather for World Cup looking good!

Yes, New Jersey was flooded on Saturday after heavy storms blanketed the area. But the good news for Sunday - and the World Cup in East Rutherford - is that the storms helped to disperse the smoke from the Canadian wildfires which had taken over the Tri-State region in recent days.

Sunday's outlook is "beautiful" for the FIFA World Cup final at MetLife Stadium, said Bill Goodman, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in New York. Highs are expected up to 85 degrees.

He added that the forecast calls for New Jersey to get its next round of thunderstorms on Tuesday.

'Hoping for the best match ever'

Matthew Velez was sitting at the White Plains Metro-North station donning an Argentina kit and headband just before 9 a.m. It’s his first World Cup final, but the second World Cup match he’s attended this year.

He went to Argentina v. Cape Verde in Miami and took the shuttle system, which he said was “the easiest way to get there.”

That was a super smooth ride and he’s hoping for the same getting to the East Rutherford Stadium today. He’ll take the subway from Grand Central to the Port Authority Bus Terminal and take the $20 shuttle to the stadium from there.

“Getting to Port Authority, that was way easier to me, you know, we’ll see how it works, I don’t know, we’ll see how it plays out, I’m hoping everything is smooth, that’s why I’m getting there early,” Velez said. “I’m just hoping for the best match ever.”

Getting to the World Cup

Kris Kolluri, who heads NJ Transit and the New Jersey Turnpike Authority, said the crowd for a World Cup final — with tickets averaging over $11,000, according to Forbes — is different than those of the seven prior matches that took place in the Meadowlands. In other words, expect more match-goers will rely on black car service as opposed to public transportation.

The window of traffic and chaos around the stadium will be longer than past matches because an opening ceremony, featuring Tom Cruise and other stars, begins at 1:30 p.m., and there will be a closing ceremony when the match ends to award the trophy.

Host committee shuttle service at its three pick-up locations in Manhattan and one in Nutley, New Jersey begins at 9:30 a.m.

For more details on transportation to the World Cup final, check here.

Argentina or Spain? Our prediction who wins World Cup

Will it be Spain or Argentina that wins the World Cup?

Lionel Messi and Argentina are able to break through for a goal, but ultimately Spain’s defense is too much to handle as Spain takes down the defending champs.

search_result.title: Spain and UNICEF stole the show: Winners, losers of World Cup final
search_result.text:
July 19, 2026, 9:22 p.m. ET

After 104 matches across 16 cities in three countries, Spain reigns supreme in the 2026 World Cup.

La Roja won the tournament by beating Argentina 1-0 in the final on Sunday, July 19 at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, N.J. This is their first title since 2010.

Lionel Messi and Argentina were neutralized and did not have a shot on goal in the entire match, which went into extra time.

After both teams won their groups and then clawed their way through the knockout rounds, a charity photo from 2007 of a young Messi giving a baby Lamine Yamal a bath went viral as a wink of destiny.

Here are the winners and losers of the World Cup final between Spain and Argentina:

Winners

Spain

If you would have told football fans that Spain was going to win the World Cup after their scoreless opening draw with newcomer Cape Verde, they would have laughed. But La Roja gutted out the tournament as one of the most well-rounded sides playing. Besides winning their second men's World Cup, which is their first since 2010, La Roja nearly ran the table with the player awards, too. AND they are the first country to hold both the men's and women's World Cup titles at the same ... darn ... time.

Emiliano Martínez

The Argentina goalkeeper had his work cut out for him as Spain dominated in possession. He broke the World Cup final record with 11 saves in the match, including diving to swat away Lamine Yamal's free kick in second half stoppage time. Even though Argentina lost, Martínez can hold his head high.

Cape Verde

Cape Verde is truly the people's champion of the 2026 World Cup. The African nation made its debut in the tournament this summer and rattled Spain in the opening match. They then had Argentina's back against the ropes in the round of 32. Knowing that they gave tough fights to the eventual runner-up and champion, the Blue Sharks have to feel good.

UNICEF

That photo of a young Lionel Messi bathing a baby Lamine Yamal was absolutely EVERYWHERE leading up to the World Cup final. It is actually from a charity photo shoot that UNICEF put together back in 2007. The non-profit was already somewhat of a household name, but this embeds them deep into sports history in a way that no publicist could ever plan.

Losers

Argentina

Argentina's late surge did not come against a Spain team that controlled the entire World Cup final. And, after a tournament riddled with controversy, the side didn't even show a glimpse of greatness in the match. Instead, their highlight reel will feature Enzo Fernández's second yellow card in the second half, which equaled a red card. He was ejected and Argentina was forced to continue with 10 players. They finished the fixture with absolutely ZERO shots on goal, far from a performance that they will want to remember.

Donald Trump

President Donald Trump was in attendance at the World Cup final along with members of his family and other dignitaries. He has attempted to position himself as an influential decision-maker in the tournament, including taking credit for having Folarin Balogun's red card rescinded. The president was booed when he came on the pitch to award the medals and trophy to Spain and then made a fool of himself by sticking around too long.

Chris Martin, FIFA, whoever's responsible for World Cup halftime show

We will always love "Yellow," but the Coldplay frontman let us down with the extremely chaotic World Cup halftime show, which he was supposedly in charge of curating. FIFA was clearly gunning for the Super Bowl with the performance, the first of its kind at the global tournament. But where the NFL is thoughtful in getting a single, or sometimes a few, popular stars to deliver an artful performance, World Cup organizers provided a disjointed, throbbing mish mash that was simply hard to watch.

search_result.title: Which teams have won two straight World Cup titles? - USA Today
search_result.text:
Updated July 19, 2026, 2:26 p.m. ET

Editor's note:Follow our LIVE Argentina vs Spain World Cup final updates

Winning a World Cup is hard. Repeating as World Cup champions has proved much more difficult.

Only eight teams have won the men's World Cup across 22 previous editions. That number will not increase in 2026 as previous winners Argentina and Spain get ready to face off in the final on Sunday, July 19.

Spain will be looking to win its second World Cup title at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, while Argentina will be aiming for its fourth.

Argentina is also looking to become just the third team to repeat as World Cup champion, and the first in more than 60 years.

Here are the only two teams that have pulled off the feat.

Italy (1934, 1938)

Led by legendary manager Vittorio Pozzo, Italy became the first repeat World Cup champion by winning the second and third edition of the tournament.

Italy won on home soil in 1934, beating Czechoslovakia in the final, then sealed a repeat in France four years later by defeating Hungary in the final.

Pozzo is still the only manager to coach a team to two men's World Cup titles. Argentina's Lionel Scaloni will look to join him on Sunday.

Brazil (1958, 1962)

Brazil defeated host nation Sweden 5-2 in the 1958 final, with a 17-year-old named Pele scoring two goals in the final in Stockholm.

Pele was injured in Brazil's second match of the 1962 World Cup, but the likes of Garrincha, Vava and Amarildo led the team to a repeat title by defeating Czechoslovakia in the final.

Women's World Cup

Though the first edition of the Women's World Cup was not held until 1991, there have been the same number of repeat champions as the men's edition.

Germany won back-to-back titles in 2003 and 2007, before the United States joined them by winning in 2015 and 2019.

July 18, 2026 Updated July 19, 2026, 9:01 p.m. ET

England and France played one of the wildest World Cup matches in history, a 6-4 England victory to secure the bronze medal at this 2026 tournament.

The 10 combined goals was the most in a World Cup game since 1982.

The Three Lions took the lead less than three minutes in with Declan Rice’s long-range goal, then Ezri Konsa headed home Rice’s corner 15 minutes later to double England’s lead. Bukayo Saka added two before the halftime whistle as England took a stunning 4-0 lead into the break.

But France wasn’t done. In his last game after 14 years in charge, Didier Deschamps made a quadruple sub to start the second half, shaking things up in attack with the additions of Ousmane Dembele and Bradley Barcola.

Kylian Mbappe scored a few minutes after the intermission, his ninth goal at this tournament to take the Golden Boot lead over Lionel Messi and 21th career World Cup score, equaling the mark Messi set this summer. Barcola scored 10 minutes later and suddenly England’s lead was down to 4-2.

Mbappe scored again in the 66th minute to pull France within one and make him the all-time leader in World Cup goals. But Saka converted a penalty in the 87th to restore the two-goal advantage. Dembele, of course, responded in stoppage time to give France hope again and make it 5-4.

But it still wasn’t over!

Substitute Jude Bellingham scored in the 98th minute to ice it for England and secure the team's best World Cup finish since winning it all in 1966.

Bukayo Saka steps forward to smash home the penalty kick after Djed Spence was fouled in the box, and the Arsenal star his hat trick. More importantly, England has a two-goal lead again.

End-to-end action

Minutes after Jude Bellingham came on, England had a major opportunity to restore a two-goal cushion but were kept out.

England subs: Bellingham and Anderson on

Hanging on for dear life, Thomas Tuchel brought on Jude Bellingham and Elliot Anderson to replace Eze and Toney in the 79th minute.

Michael Olise sets assist record

France's Michael Olise was credited with assists on both of Kylian Mbappe's goals and now has seven assists at this World Cup, breaking Pele's record for most in a single tournament.

Mbappe goal again!

It's 4-3 now in Miami after Kylian Mbappe scored his second goal o the game in the 67th minute, his 10th at this World Cup and 22nd career in the World Cup, breaking a tie with Lionel Messi.

Both teams pushing hard for more

This game has opened up in the second half with France pouring numbers forward and England getting opportunities to create space on the counter-attack, still up 4-2 in the 65th minute.

Les Bleus have halved England's lead with two goals in the first 10 minutes of the second half, the latter through Bradley Barcola.

Game on in Miami!

Kylian Mbappe goal!

Mbappe scores in the 48th minute to take the 2026 Golden Boot lead and tie Lionel Messi with his 21st career World Cup goal.

Ollie Watkins replaces Rashford

Thomas Tuchel made his own substitution to start the second half, bringing on Ollie Watkins for Marcus Rashford.

Quadruple sub for France

Dembele, Digne, Barcola and Upamecano replace Konate, Doue, Hernandez and Cherki as the teams take the field for the second half.

HALFTIME: England leads 4-0

That was not what we were expecting in Miami! The Three Lions head into the intermission up 4-0 behind two goals from Buakyo Saka and one from Declan Rice and Ezri Konsa.

In the first half, Arsenal players accounted for three goals (Saka and Rice) and two assists (Eberechi Eze and Rice).

Bukayo Saka goal! England 3, France 0

An absolutely bonkers counter-attack ends with Bukayo Saka smashing home on a mostly-open net, staking England to. a3-0 lead in the 37th minute.

Ezri Konsa goal! England 2, France 0

Ezri Konsa headed Declan Rice's corner kick to the far post in the 18th minute, extending England's lead to 2-0.

That's Konsa's second international goal, the first coming in a World Cup qualifier against Serbia in 2025.

Offside erases Saka goal

England's Bukayo Saka appeared to have scored his team's second goal after a mazy run down the right side, but the flag went up for offside.

10 minutes in: England 1, France 0

Declan Rice's goal in the third minute remains the only score, but both teams have looked positive in the first 10 minutes, particularly England pushing forward with a front line of Marcus Rashford, Ivan Toney and Bukayo Saka.

Less than three minutes into the match, Declan Rice stepped up and scored a long-range goal, his first of this World Cup to put England ahead on France.

"You who have given us so much, we should have offered you a better ending but we failed," Mbappé wrote. "To put into words all that you have brought us for the past 14 years is very difficult. You have been such a major player in the rebuilding of this team. People didn’t always know how to appreciate your greatness, but time and history will change all of that."

The clashing of two stars

This match had been billed as Kylian Mbappé vs. Messi – the 23-year-old French star ready to assume the mantle of the world’s greatest player from his 35-year-old Paris Saint-Germain teammate.

Mbappé was defending France’s 2018 win at the tournament in Russia, Messi was playing in his final World Cup match, looking to claim the trophy which has eluded him for so long and which would enable him to match Diego Maradona’s achievement of winning the 1986 competition.

The opening 79 minutes was all about Messi. Argentina’s captain converted the penalty to give Argentina the lead. Next, his deft touch was key in springing the move which led to La Albiceleste’s second.

Then in the closing stages of normal time, Mbappé single-handedly took a grip of the game, scoring two goals in two minutes and sending the final to extra time.

Messi looked shot and Mbappé looked like he was just getting going.

Except it was the diminutive Argentine who next popped up to score his second goal of the match and restore his team’s lead in the 109th minute.

Refusing to accept defeat, Mbappé roused his teammates, scoring a second penalty to grab his hat-trick and take the final to a penalty shootout.

Both Mbappé and Messi scored in the shootout but in the end – with France missing two penalties – it was the Argentina captain who was mobbed by his teammates as his World Cup dream was lived out in real time.

Over two hours of soccer, these was two players – at two different points of their careers – demonstrating the beautiful game in vivid, glorious technicolor.

Mbappé sits on the bench at the end of the World Cup final. Manu Fernandez/AP

From the spot

The last time a World Cup final went to penalties was in 2006 when France was once again beaten, this time by Italy.

Sometimes, it feels unfair to settle a game in a shootout, a series of actions between the penalty taker and the goalkeeper.

However, at the Lusail Stadium on Sunday, the abundance of penalties seemed to ratchet up the pressure and tension.

Messi’s penalty in the first half gave him his first World Cup final goal, while his spot kick in the shootout was coolness personified.

Mbappé’s ability to not once, not twice, but three times successfully convert from the spot in one game showed extreme gumption.

Mbappé scores France's third goal against Argentina in the World Cup final. Clive Brunskill/Getty Images

Previously at Qatar 2022, one team had already experienced the intensity of that pressure cooker atmosphere and emerged the other side, and one which had not.

Argentina got the better of the Netherlands in the quarterfinals in an epic which culminated in a penalty shootout, and one which saw the South American team display distraction and delaying tactics to arguably mentally monster their opponents.

In Sunday’s final, Argentina goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez showing his ability to distract the French takers, throwing the ball away before Aurélien Tchouaméni attempt, which flew wide. France’s previous attempt – from Kingsley Coman – had been saved by Martinez.

A penalty shootout is arguably unlike anything else in sports – it’s a modern day duel and a World Cup final with so much at stake only heightens the tension and drama.

Martínez saves the penalty from Kingsley Coman of France in the World Cup final. Simon Stacpoole/Offside/Getty Images

Great goals

World Cup finals are often tight and cagey affairs, with goals at a premium.

Argentina and France threw away that playbook – delivering six goals, two of which were of the highest quality.

Argentina’s second was arguably as good as Carlos Alberto’s breathtaking goal in the 1970 World Cup final in Brazil’s 4-1 win over Italy.

It was in the 35th minute, when a flick round the corner from Alexis Mac Allister to Messi, relieved some pressure on the Argentina defense as France pushed for an equalizer.

After Messi’s deft touch to Julián Álvarez and the Manchester City forward’s excellently weighted pass to Mac Allister, who had continued his run, Argentina was in on goal.

Unselfishly, Mac Allister had the presence of mind to square the ball to Ángel Di María who finished off a brilliant sweeping counterattack to put Argentina 2-0 up.

Di María celebrates after he scored Argentina's second goal against France in the World Cup final. Stefan Matzke/sampics/Corbis Sport/Getty Images

At that point, it looked to be the crowning moment of a dominant Argentina victory, until Mbappé stepped up.

After his penalty reduced the deficit to 2-1, a neat one-two with Marcus Thuram had the ball falling to the PSG star out of the sky on the edge of Argentina’s penalty area.

With seemingly all the time in the world, Mbappé produced a wonderful display of technique and timing to thunder the ball past a despairing Martínez.

These are the moments that capture imaginations and the moments that came to define the 2022 World Cup final.

It will be remembered for so many reasons – Messi’s moment of history, Mbappé’s hat-trick in defeat, the seesaw nature of the game that oscillated from end to end and never ceased to tug on gobsmacked watchers’ emotions.

Other great World Cup finals

Of course, there’s plenty of competition for the title of ‘greatest World Cup final.’

In 1950, Uruguay upset Brazil in Rio de Janeiro, while four years later, West Germany provided another huge surprise, beating Hungary’s Magical Magyars, earning the country its first World Cup title.

Geoff Hurst scored the first World Cup final hat-trick in the 1966 final between England and West Germany. Hurst’s second goal is still talked about 56 years later – had the ball crossed the line? It did, according to the game’s officials and England won 4-2.

The 1970 final marked Pelé’s last World Cup appearance as he secured his third title in Brazil’s swashbuckling victory over Italy.

Four years later in Munich, host West Germany came from behind to win 2-1 against a star-studded Netherlands team – made up of Johan Cruyff and Johan Neeskens – to win its second World Cup.

Much like Messi at Qatar 2022, Diego Maradona almost single-handedly drove his team to its second title in eight years, beating West Germany 3-2 in the final.

In 1998, France hosted and won its first World Cup, mainly down to the genius of Zinedine Zidane, who scored twice in the final, to beat a formidable Brazil side, composed of Ronaldo, Rivaldo, Cafu, Bebeto and Roberto Carlos.

However, with its multiples story lines and the drama and artistry on display, surely the 2022 showpiece now owns the title of ‘greatest World Cup final.’
